name: JRC/GHSL/P2023A/GHS_BUILT_S and the wider Global Human Settlement Layer

identity.method_name: Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL), P2023A / R2023A release -- built-up surface, height, volume and population products
identity.core_idea: GHSL is a family of global gridded layers produced by the EU Joint Research Centre that classify and quantify the built environment (surface area, height, volume) and population, derived from Landsat (1975, 1990, 2000, 2014) and Sentinel-2 (2018) imagery classification, then spatially and temporally interpolated/extrapolated onto a common 5-year epoch grid running from 1975 to 2030. It is a modelled, globally-consistent reconstruction of urban growth, not a per-year direct satellite observation for most of its published years.
identity.official_dataset_ids: JRC/GHSL/P2023A/GHS_BUILT_S (built-up surface, m^2 per 100 m cell, multitemporal 1975-2030 in 5-year steps; bands built_surface, built_surface_nres); JRC/GHSL/P2023A/GHS_BUILT_S_10m (built-up surface, 10 m grid, single epoch 2018 only; bands built_surface, built_surface_nres); JRC/GHSL/P2023A/GHS_BUILT_H (building height, 100 m grid, single epoch 2018 only; band built_height); JRC/GHSL/P2023A/GHS_BUILT_V (building volume, m^3 per 100 m cell, multitemporal 1975-2030 in 5-year steps; bands built_volume_total, built_volume_nres); JRC/GHSL/P2023A/GHS_POP (population grid, multitemporal 1975-2030 in 5-year steps); JRC/GHSL/P2023A/GHS_SMOD_V2-0 (Degree of Urbanisation settlement model, multitemporal 1975-2030); related but distinct 10 m functional layer JRC/GHSL/P2023A/GHS_BUILT_C (settlement characteristics, single epoch 2018).

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Not a labelling strategy -- like item D1, this is an external, already-modelled data source that could at most supply an engineered covariate (catchment-scale built-up surface/volume near each lake). It does not produce an encroachment label, and because GHSL is itself the output of JRC's own classification-plus-interpolation model, using it as an input feature to the project's own model means chaining one unvalidated model's predictions into another, with no ground truth check at any stage.
fit_to_project.input_required: A catchment-scale ring or study-area polygon around each lake (not the 30 m legal buffer -- see resolution_match_20m) and access to Google Earth Engine or the JRC data portal to pull GHS_BUILT_S/H/V values for the relevant epoch(s). The project does not currently ingest GHSL and would need a new extraction step; critically, it would also need to define a coarser catchment polygon than the project's existing 30 m buffer, since the buffer itself is not usable with this data (see below).
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: only-if-reframed, and only partially even then. Using the official 5-year epoch grid, only 2 of the project's 7 years (2020, 2025) have any GHS_BUILT_S/V value at all, giving at most 6 lakes x 2 years = 12 of 42 rows populated, all at catchment scale. Using JRC's officially-described annual linear-interpolation product instead could in principle populate all 6 lakes x 7 years = 42 rows, but every value for a year after the last truly observed epoch (2018) is by construction a linear interpolation or forward extrapolation, not a measurement -- so even a 'complete' 42-row matrix from GHSL would be 42 modelled numbers, not 42 observations.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes -- no labels are needed to query a pre-existing gridded product, but see the ground_truth_proxy_strategy caveat about compounding one model's unverified output into another.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: No, and this is the central finding of this item. GHS_BUILT_S/H/V are natively 100 m grid cells; the project's Sentinel-2 grid is 20 m, so one GHSL cell spans exactly 5x5 = 25 of the project's own pixels. Far more importantly for the project's stated geo-fencing goal, the legal buffer under test is 30 m wide -- less than one-third the width (30/100 = 0.3) of a single GHSL cell. A 30 m buffer ring around a lake will frequently be entirely contained within, or only marginally overlap, a single 100 m GHSL pixel. It is therefore not mathematically meaningful to compute 'percentage of the 30 m buffer that is built up' from GHS_BUILT_S: the number produced would be a fixed areal share of one coarse pixel's already-aggregated value, not a measurement of what is actually built inside that specific 30 m ring. The 10 m variant (GHS_BUILT_S_10m) resolves this spatial problem but only for a single frozen 2018 snapshot -- it trades away the multitemporal dimension entirely, so it cannot supply a resolution fix and a per-year fix simultaneously. Plain statement: GHSL cannot be used for buffer-level intrusion detection at these six lakes; it can only speak to catchment-scale (hundreds of metres to kilometres) built-up pressure around each lake.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Only very partially addresses limitation (2). It would replace the constant OSM snapshot with, at best, two real epoch time points (2020, 2025) or a fully-interpolated annual series -- but only at catchment scale, never at the buffer scale where the project's geo-fencing deliverable actually operates, and the 2020/2025 values themselves are modelled fill/extrapolation rather than direct observations (see temporal_granularity). It does not address limitations (1), (3) or (4).
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No -- built-up surface/height/volume says nothing about the lake's own water extent and cannot distinguish a desilting drawdown from encroachment; this is entirely orthogonal to GHSL's subject matter.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: Not applicable / no interaction -- GHSL classifies land built-up area, not water-surface vegetation, so it neither helps nor interferes with the Bellandur/Varthur hyacinth-vs-open-water confusion.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None, and less usable than item D1 for this purpose. Even setting aside the missing legal reference, the 100 m grid cannot be intersected with the 30 m Master Plan/KTCDA buffer or the 75 m historic NGT buffer in any way that produces a defensible per-lake number -- both candidate buffer widths (30 m and 75 m) are smaller than, or only slightly larger than, one GHSL cell edge. Any legal-buffer-level claim built on GHS_BUILT_S would be a resampling artefact dressed up as a measurement, not evidence traceable to the buffer geometry.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Officially 5-year epochs (1975, 1980, ..., 2020, 2025, 2030); of the project's 7 study years, only 2020 and 2025 land on this grid, while 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024 do not exist as GHSL epochs at all. Worse, of the 5 sensor-classified reference epochs actually used to build the whole 1975-2030 series (Landsat for 1975/1990/2000/2014, Sentinel-2 composite for 2018), NONE is 2020 or 2025 -- both of the project's in-window epochs are themselves already derived by JRC's own spatio-temporal interpolation (2020, produced by pixel-wise linear interpolation between the observed 2018 epoch and later reference points) or extrapolation (2025, produced by a rank-optimal spatial-allocation/extrapolation model projecting beyond the last observed 2018 epoch, since 2025 itself had not occurred at the time of the P2023A release). JRC does describe an official annual-interpolated derivative ('a pixel-wise linear interpolation between consecutive reference years produces an annual, globally consistent built-surface time series'), so an annual product genuinely exists and is a real, documented JRC output -- but it is explicitly a linear-interpolation/extrapolation fill for every year that is not one of the five sensor-observed epochs, i.e. for every single year in the project's 2019-2025 window. None of the project's 7 years is a raw classified observation in this dataset.

implementation.libraries: earthengine-api / geemap (ee.Image('JRC/GHSL/P2023A/GHS_BUILT_S/2020') style per-epoch access), or direct GeoTIFF download from the JRC FTP (jeodpp.jrc.ec.europa.eu) via requests/rasterio, plus geopandas/rasterstats for zonal statistics over a catchment polygon (not the 30 m buffer).
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not applicable in a form the student would use directly -- GHSL layers are precomputed rasters served by JRC/Earth Engine. The underlying production pipeline mixes a Symbolic Machine Learning classifier and CNN-based classifiers on Landsat/Sentinel-2 composites plus a separate spatial-interpolation/extrapolation model; none of this is retrainable or fine-tunable by the project, nor would there be any reason to.
implementation.licence: European Commission 'open and free data,' reuse authorised with source attribution per the EC Reuse and Copyright Notice -- functionally CC-BY-equivalent and fine for academic use; no licence blocker.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial -- reading a handful of precomputed 100 m rasters and running zonal statistics over 6 catchment polygons for 2 epochs (or 7 interpolated years) takes seconds to minutes on a laptop CPU. No GPU or Colab/Kaggle quota needed.
implementation.student_days: About 0.5-1 day to extract GHS_BUILT_S (and optionally H/V) values at the 2020/2025 epochs or the annual-interpolated series for a defined catchment ring per lake; an additional 0.5 day is realistically needed just to work through and document the buffer-vs-cell-size mismatch so the limitation is stated correctly in the write-up rather than glossed over.

evaluation.metrics: Not a predictive method to be scored; if used at all, it should be reported purely as a descriptive catchment-scale covariate (e.g. total built-up surface within 500 m-1 km of each lake, by epoch), never as an accuracy-scored intrusion detector, since the resolution mismatch makes any buffer-level accuracy claim meaningless by construction.
evaluation.validation_protocol: If a catchment-scale GHSL feature is folded into a downstream predictive model, that model still needs leave-one-lake-out validation like every other feature in this project. For the GHSL layer itself there is no train/test split to speak of -- the correct check is a plausibility audit (does the catchment built-up trend match what is known qualitatively about Bengaluru's urban growth in that decade) rather than a quantitative validation against this specific project's lakes.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Because 100 m cells aggregate a wide, slowly-changing, largely city-wide urbanisation signal, a catchment-scale GHSL feature risks being an even purer form of the 'lake identity' leakage the project is trying to eliminate than the original OSM count: it varies little year to year, is highly spatially autocorrelated across nearby lakes in the same part of the city, and could let a model learn 'this background built-up level = Bellandur' almost as directly as a static building count would. This is a real risk of reintroducing, not fixing, the diagnosed problem.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: No per-pixel uncertainty layer is distributed with GHS_BUILT_S. The only published validation figure found is an aggregate global correlation (Pearson r roughly 0.81 for built-up-fraction prediction against ~50,000 globally-representative test cells [verify -- figure drawn from a secondary summary of the R2023A validation report, not independently confirmed against the primary JRC validation table]), which says nothing about local (Bengaluru) accuracy, and nothing about the additional, unquantified error introduced by the linear-interpolation/extrapolation step needed to reach 2020 or 2025. Any catchment number derived from GHSL for these lakes should be reported as an unquantified-uncertainty point estimate, with this compounding-model caveat stated explicitly.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable in the synthetic-data-augmentation sense, but a closely analogous honesty risk exists: presenting GHSL's linearly-interpolated or extrapolated 2020/2025 (or full annual) values as if they were seven independent yearly observations, rather than disclosing them as modelled infill of a 5-year-epoch product, would be functionally equivalent to fabricating a data point and must be avoided or explicitly flagged wherever shown.

evidence.published_performance: R2023A validation reportedly found a Pearson correlation coefficient of approximately 0.81 for built-up-fraction (BUFRAC) prediction against a globally-representative set of roughly 50,000 test cells [verify -- drawn from a secondary summary, not the primary JRC validation report table]. A separate, independent accuracy assessment of an earlier GHSL vintage over China (Liu et al., PLOS ONE, 2020, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0233164) found GHSL 'validated only in the United States and European countries' with a documented tendency to underestimate low-density built-up areas and overestimate high-density ones, explicitly cautioning that US/European validation results cannot guarantee accuracy in Asia [verify -- this paper assessed an older GHSL release, not confirmed to be R2023A specifically, so its numeric figures should not be read as current R2023A accuracy, only as a documented regional-transfer caveat].
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: Global aggregate validation (~50,000 worldwide sample cells) for the headline correlation figure; the China accuracy paper is national-scale for China, not India, and not lake- or Bengaluru-specific. No study found validates GHS_BUILT_S accuracy specifically for Bengaluru or for water-body-adjacent land.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No peer-reviewed application of GHSL to Bengaluru lakes or Indian urban lake buffers specifically was located in this research [verify -- absence of evidence, not confirmed absence]. GHSL is widely used in broad South/Southeast Asian urbanisation and population-exposure studies, but none identified here operate at the individual-lake, buffer-zone scale this project needs.
evidence.evidence_recency: R2023A / P2023A release: 2023. Core methodology paper: Pesaresi et al., "Advances on the Global Human Settlement Layer by joint assessment of Earth Observation and population survey data," International Journal of Digital Earth, 17(1), 2024. The China regional-accuracy caveat (Liu et al., 2020) is older and assessed a prior GHSL vintage, not R2023A directly -- flagged as the weaker, pre-2023 leg of the evidence base.

risk.failure_modes: (1) Treating the 2020 and 2025 GHSL epochs as real observations when both are, by JRC's own stated methodology, interpolated (2020) or extrapolated (2025) model output -- the 2025 value in particular was necessarily produced before 2025 occurred. (2) Attempting to compute a buffer-level 'percent built-up' figure by intersecting a 30 m ring with 100 m GHSL cells, producing a spuriously precise number that is really just an areal share of one coarse pixel. (3) Using catchment-scale GHSL trends as if they were lake-specific encroachment evidence, when they mostly track city-wide urban growth common to every lake in the district -- this risks reinforcing, not curing, the 'model memorises which lake it's looking at' problem the whole item exists to fix, because a coarse, slow-moving, near-constant-per-locale covariate is exactly the kind of feature that lets a model shortcut to lake identity. (4) Layering GHSL's own unvalidated-in-Asia model output as an input feature into the project's own model chains two unverified models together with no ground truth at either stage.
risk.panel_defensibility: Any panel member with remote-sensing exposure will ask 'your legal buffer is 30 m -- how do you use a 100 m dataset for that?' The only defensible answer is to state plainly that GHSL is not used for buffer-level results at all, only as an optional, heavily caveated catchment-scale backdrop variable. A second predictable question -- 'is your 2025 GHSL number real?' -- must be answered honestly: no, it is a pre-2025 extrapolation, not a measurement, and should be labelled as such wherever cited.
risk.honest_expectation: GHSL cannot deliver a per-year, buffer-scale built-up signal for these six lakes under any honest use of the data; its resolution is categorically too coarse (100 m cell versus a 30 m buffer) and its temporal coverage in the project window (2019-2025) is entirely modelled fill (interpolation for 2020, extrapolation for 2025, and no epoch at all for 2019/2021/2022/2023/2024). The realistic, defensible use is as a rough, heavily caveated, catchment-scale (hundreds of metres to kilometres) urbanisation-pressure backdrop variable -- not as evidence of intrusion at any specific lake, and not as a fix for the stated limitation. This is a valid null result for the buffer-level question the item was asked to answer.

verdict.recommended_rank: reject for buffer-level intrusion detection (the resolution mismatch is structural, not a matter of careful use); consider-with-reasons only as an optional, clearly-labelled, catchment-scale urbanisation-pressure control variable, and never presented as a fix for limitation (2).
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: GHSL's 100 m grid cannot see anything at the scale of our 30 m legal buffer -- the buffer is a third the width of a single GHSL pixel -- and even its 2020/2025 values are interpolated or extrapolated model output rather than real observations, so it cannot fix our constant-building-count problem and at most offers a rough, heavily caveated city-wide backdrop variable.
